A mixed-effects fit estimates population parameters: the fixed effects
`theta`, the between-subject variances `Omega` and the residual error
`sigma`.  Each subject's random effects `eta` are not parameters of the
model.  Given the data `y_i` of subject `i`, they have a whole distribution,
the *conditional* (posterior) distribution

    p(eta_i | y_i, theta, Omega, sigma)  proportional to  p(y_i | eta_i, theta, sigma) p(eta_i | Omega)

The first factor is the subject's likelihood and the second is the
population (prior) distribution of the random effects.  Every number reported
for an individual, the "individual estimates" or EBEs, summarizes this one
distribution.  This vignette shows the summaries `nlmixr2est` reports, and
how `addCondDist()` gives the distribution itself for a fit from any
estimation method.

## Point summaries: mode, mean and median

The conditional distribution has three common point summaries:

- the **mode**, the most likely `eta_i`.  It is what FOCEi, `"laplace"` and
  `"agq"` report as `fit$eta`, because their inner problem maximizes the
  conditional density.  `"foce"` reports an approximate mode: its inner
  problem holds the residual variance at its `eta = 0` value.  SAEM
  reports it as `fit$eta` too (`saemControl(ebe = "mode")`, the default),
  searching for it after the last iteration;
- the **mean**, the average `eta_i`.  SAEM approximates it while it
  estimates: its MCMC chains sample the conditional distribution, and their
  stochastic-approximation average is kept as `fit$etaSaem`
  (`saemControl(ebe = "saem")` reports it as `fit$eta` instead);
- the **median**, which `addCondDist()` gives from the sampled draws.

When the model is close to linear in `eta` and the data are informative, the
conditional distribution is nearly normal and all three agree.  They diverge
for sparse data or a strongly non-linear model.

## The conditional distribution of any fit

The conditional distribution depends only on the model and the final
`theta`, `Omega` and `sigma`, not on how they were estimated.  So it can be
sampled for a fit from any method: hold the population parameters at the
fit's estimates and simulate each subject's `eta_i` from the density above.
`addCondDist()` has two samplers:

- `method = "imp"` (the default except for SAEM) draws importance samples
  from a normal proposal centered at each subject's mode, with the Laplace
  (inverse Hessian) covariance, and weights each one by its posterior
  density.  It is the frozen E-step of `est = "imp"` and works for any model
  the FOCEi inner problem handles.  The `"ess"` attribute is each subject's
  effective sample size: a value far below `nsamp` means the proposal fits
  the posterior poorly;
- `method = "saem"` (the default for SAEM) uses SAEM's MCMC kernels.  A SAEM
  fit already ran them at (nearly) its final estimates, so the draws of its
  last iterations, from the last half of its second phase, are used
  directly and nothing is simulated.  When those
  are not enough, or for a fit from another method, the kernels are run
  again with every population parameter held at the fit's estimates.

`fit$condDist` holds each subject's conditional mean (`MEAN`) and SD (`SD`);
`keepSamples = TRUE` keeps equally weighted draws as its `"samples"`
attribute.

### A FOCEi fit


``` r
library(nlmixr2est)

one.cmt <- function() {
  ini({
    tka <- 0.45
    tcl <- 1
    tv <- 3.45
    eta.ka ~ 0.6
    eta.cl ~ 0.3
    eta.v ~ 0.1
    add.sd <- 0.7
  })
  model({
    ka <- exp(tka + eta.ka)
    cl <- exp(tcl + eta.cl)
    v <- exp(tv + eta.v)
    linCmt() ~ add(add.sd)
  })
}

fit <- nlmixr2(one.cmt, nlmixr2data::theo_sd, est = "focei",
               control = foceiControl(print = 0))
fit <- addCondDist(fit, keepSamples = TRUE)
head(fit$condDist)
#>   ID    ETA         MEAN         SD
#> 1  1 eta.ka  0.086724343 0.13290765
#> 2  1 eta.cl -0.485157088 0.09737933
#> 3  1  eta.v -0.089112392 0.04531539
#> 4  2 eta.ka  0.198230689 0.15866379
#> 5  2 eta.cl  0.144418922 0.09494652
#> 6  2  eta.v  0.005335317 0.06765941
attr(fit$condDist, "method")
#> [1] "imp"
round(attr(fit$condDist, "ess"))
#>  [1] 215 192 206 213 199 205 209 208 213 205 204 207
```

The mode (`fit$eta`), the conditional mean and the conditional median of
`eta.ka` side by side:


``` r
cd <- fit$condDist
draws <- attr(cd, "samples")
data.frame(
  ID = fit$eta$ID,
  mode = fit$eta$eta.ka,
  mean = cd$MEAN[cd$ETA == "eta.ka"],
  median = apply(draws[, "eta.ka", ], 1, median),
  sd = cd$SD[cd$ETA == "eta.ka"]
)
#>    ID        mode        mean      median        sd
#> 1   1  0.08483290  0.08672434  0.08770607 0.1329077
#> 2   2  0.19668530  0.19823069  0.19838253 0.1586638
#> 3   3  0.37074077  0.38222137  0.37349500 0.1835270
#> 4   4 -0.28326871 -0.29426053 -0.29504895 0.1561942
#> 5   5 -0.04451592 -0.02423361 -0.01101069 0.1229863
#> 6   6 -0.38629405 -0.36181502 -0.34906878 0.2017724
#> 7   7 -0.77308932 -0.77026747 -0.75481550 0.1899175
#> 8   8 -0.16884271 -0.16554042 -0.18128449 0.1806589
#> 9   9  1.36248859  1.42805547  1.42121026 0.2460347
#> 10 10 -0.73460315 -0.74336911 -0.72809855 0.1390726
#> 11 11  0.75352200  0.78498173  0.78351873 0.1971994
#> 12 12 -0.52166457 -0.52220798 -0.52943903 0.1295458
```

The `SD` column is the uncertainty of each subject's estimate, which a
single point summary does not show.  A 90% interval comes from the draws:


``` r
t(apply(draws[, "eta.cl", ], 1, quantile, c(0.05, 0.95)))
#>             5%         95%
#> 1  -0.65771769 -0.33075773
#> 2  -0.01824719  0.28685044
#> 3  -0.17200425  0.15512269
#> 4  -0.19597461  0.12645975
#> 5  -0.29249574 -0.01762039
#> 6   0.13834034  0.56339110
#> 7  -0.07237582  0.32263351
#> 8  -0.04182502  0.34061706
#> 9  -0.13971613  0.22271590
#> 10 -0.56880964 -0.24860321
#> 11  0.11067063  0.46515669
#> 12 -0.27603296  0.01223934
```

### Shrinkage

When a subject's data say little about an eta, its conditional distribution
stays close to the prior and its point estimate is pulled toward 0.  The
usual eta shrinkage, `fit$shrink`, measures this from the spread of the
point estimates, `1 - SD(eta_i) / sqrt(omega)` (in %).  The conditional
distribution gives it directly: by the law of total variance,

    omega = E(Var(eta_i | y_i)) + Var(E(eta_i | y_i))

so the share of `omega` the data do not explain is the average conditional
variance over `omega`.  `fit$condDistShrinkage` is that share,
`100 * mean(SD^2) / omega`, a variance shrinkage that does not depend on the
spread of shrunk point estimates:


``` r
fit$condDistShrinkage
#>    eta.ka    eta.cl     eta.v 
#>  7.462363 15.386708 23.814288
```

### Diagnostics from shrunk estimates

Point estimates are a poor basis for diagnostics on `Omega`.  Shrinkage
pulls them toward 0, so their spread understates the between-subject
variability, and because each subject's etas are shrunk by the same data,
their correlations can be distorted too.  Draws from the conditional
distribution, pooled over subjects, are not shrunk: by the same law of total
variance their covariance estimates `Omega` itself.


``` r
pooled <- apply(draws, 2, as.vector)
rbind(
  omega = diag(fit$omega),
  modes = apply(fit$eta[, -1], 2, var),
  draws = apply(pooled, 2, var)
)
#>          eta.ka     eta.cl      eta.v
#> omega 0.4031402 0.06963923 0.01933736
#> modes 0.3886518 0.06389900 0.01547284
#> draws 0.4063483 0.07017849 0.01916460
round(cor(fit$eta[, -1]), 2)
#>        eta.ka eta.cl eta.v
#> eta.ka   1.00   0.20  0.26
#> eta.cl   0.20   1.00  0.85
#> eta.v    0.26   0.85  1.00
round(cor(pooled), 2)
#>        eta.ka eta.cl eta.v
#> eta.ka   1.00   0.16  0.31
#> eta.cl   0.16   1.00  0.59
#> eta.v    0.31   0.59  1.00
```

With only 12 subjects both are rough, but the modes' variances fall short of
`Omega`, most for the most shrunk `eta.v`, while the draws' do not.  The
modes also suggest a strong `eta.cl`-`eta.v` correlation that the draws,
which carry each subject's uncertainty as well, show to be weaker.

## A SAEM fit

SAEM reports two point summaries: the conditional mode as `fit$eta` and its
approximate conditional mean as `fit$etaSaem`.  `addCondDist()` reads the
conditional distribution from the fit's own chains:


``` r
fitS <- nlmixr2(one.cmt, nlmixr2data::theo_sd, est = "saem",
                control = saemControl(print = 0))
fitS <- addCondDist(fitS)
attr(fitS$condDist, "method")
#> [1] "saem"
cdS <- fitS$condDist
data.frame(
  ID = fitS$eta$ID,
  mode = fitS$eta$eta.cl,
  etaSaem = fitS$etaSaem$eta.cl,
  mean = cdS$MEAN[cdS$ETA == "eta.cl"],
  sd = cdS$SD[cdS$ETA == "eta.cl"]
)
#>    ID        mode     etaSaem        mean         sd
#> 1   1 -0.47434190 -0.47574170 -0.47469337 0.09570751
#> 2   2  0.14458822  0.13286293  0.13908906 0.10184931
#> 3   3  0.02863249  0.02409061  0.01619569 0.09929586
#> 4   4 -0.01759252 -0.01655285 -0.02135252 0.10073345
#> 5   5 -0.15037205 -0.15614017 -0.15636640 0.08536285
#> 6   6  0.37505251  0.36097884  0.36117667 0.13588735
#> 7   7  0.14822171  0.13547018  0.14809598 0.12004372
#> 8   8  0.16612395  0.16077843  0.16232261 0.11544291
#> 9   9  0.04538024  0.04501904  0.04294496 0.09518125
#> 10 10 -0.38188484 -0.39258109 -0.39777296 0.09819460
#> 11 11  0.28857341  0.27669803  0.28217101 0.10672826
#> 12 12 -0.12555411 -0.12945705 -0.11804624 0.09094826
```

`fit$etaSaem` averages the chains over iterations whose population
parameters were still moving, so it can be noisier than the conditional mean
at the final estimates.  The importance sampler gives the same distribution for
the SAEM fit:


``` r
cdI <- addCondDist(fitS, method = "imp")$condDist
summary(abs(cdI$MEAN - cdS$MEAN) / cdS$SD)
#>     Min.  1st Qu.   Median     Mean  3rd Qu.     Max. 
#> 0.008031 0.040827 0.057627 0.089992 0.125410 0.233920
summary(cdI$SD / cdS$SD)
#>    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
#>  0.8791  0.9709  0.9999  0.9995  1.0289  1.1406
```

## Notes

- `nsamp` (default 300) is the number of draws per subject; the Monte-Carlo
  error of a conditional mean is about `SD / sqrt(ESS)`.
- The samplers are seeded (`seed`), so `addCondDist()` is reproducible.
- An eta SAEM does not sample for a subject (an uninformative eta) has
  `SD` `NA` and `MEAN` 0, its prior; the shrinkage counts it as fully
  shrunk.  Both are exact when that eta is uncorrelated with the others.
- Mixture, inter-occasion variability and non-parametric (`"npag"`,
  `"npb"`, ...) fits are not supported yet.  A non-parametric fit's random
  effects follow its discrete support, not `Omega`.
